meta.title: The Tree in the Wind
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer stays close to one small sound, then widens out to the whole forest.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 115w at FK 5.9, part_2 106w at FK 6.2, part_3 108w at FK 6.5, with mean sentences of 15 to 18 words. The load is a change of scale: one leaf and one needle, then a whole range of trees.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from John Muir, The Mountains of California (1894), chapter X, 'A Wind-Storm in the Forests', under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: John Muir. The Mountains of California. 1894. Project Gutenberg eBook #10012, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10012, accessed 2026-11-12. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, dropped rare words and simplified technical terms; no facts added.
source.survey: The storm chapter of The Mountains of California: the climb to the ridge, the choice of a tree, the sounds close to the ear, and the forest seen from the top.
source.avoided: No invented details. Muir's comparisons to Aeolian harps and his closing reflections are left out to keep the passage on the one move.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot-adjacent, adapted from the named human source

session.difficulty_basis: the writer's move from one small sound to a view of the whole forest

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: In December 1874 I was walking in a side valley of the Yuba River. The rain had washed the woods, and then the sky cleared into one of those warm California winter days. The air was full of white, sparkling sunshine, and the whole forest was already moving. I climbed to the top of the highest ridge so that I could hear the storm better. From there I saw that the wind did not push in one steady stream. It came in long, rolling sweeps that bent the pines and then let them spring back again. I stood in the wind for a while and listened, and then I decided to climb one of the trees.
passage.part_2: The choice of a tree was a serious matter, because a dead top would have broken in the first strong gust. I picked a sound one and climbed until my head was among its topmost needles. Up there the sound came apart into separate pieces. I could hear the quick, tense vibration of the needles, rising to a thin whistle and then falling away to a soft murmur. I could hear the rustle of the laurel leaves in the hollows below me. I could hear the small, hard click of one leaf against another, over and over, close to my ear. Nothing was mixed together yet.
passage.part_3: Then I looked out, and all those single sounds joined into one. The trees below me were swinging together, and I could tell the kinds apart by the way each one moved. Spruce, fir, pine, and leafless oak each had its own gesture, and I could name a tree by that gesture at a distance of several miles. The whole range was moving at once, and every tree in it was answering the same wind. I stayed in my perch for hours, sometimes closing my eyes so that I could hear the music by itself. It sounded like the sea, and I did not want to climb down.

items.prompt: In December 1874, where was the writer walking?

tutor_only.confirm: He was walking in a side valley of the Yuba River.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The first sentence gives the place: 'In December 1874 I was walking in a side valley of the Yuba River.'
tutor_only.tell: The opening says he was walking in a side valley of the Yuba River.
help: The first sentence names the river and the valley.
The month and the place are given together in that sentence.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer was walking in a side valley of the Yuba River.
accept_ideas: in a side valley of the Yuba River
a valley off the Yuba River
a tributary valley of the Yuba River
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They name only the state or the mountains, such as California or the Sierra.
partial.ask: Which valley and which river does the writer name?

if_they_say.when: They say he was walking in a forest without naming any river.
if_they_say.ask: The writer names a river. Which one?

items.prompt: The writer says the wind did not push in one steady stream. How did it come instead?

tutor_only.confirm: It came in long, rolling sweeps that bent the pines and let them spring back.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence about the wind says it 'came in long, rolling sweeps that bent the pines and then let them spring back again.'
tutor_only.tell: The wind came in long, rolling sweeps that bent the pines and let them spring back.
help: The sentence about the wind describes its shape, not its speed.
The pines bend and then come back up.
tutor_only.core_idea: The wind came in long, rolling sweeps that bent the pines and let them spring back.
accept_ideas: in rolling gusts that bent the trees and let them spring back
in sweeps that bent the pines and then released them
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the wind blew harder and harder without describing its shape.
partial.ask: What shape did the wind take as it crossed the trees?

if_they_say.when: They say the wind stopped and started again.
if_they_say.ask: Did the wind stop, or did it roll through in sweeps?

items.prompt: The writer could name a tree 'at a distance of several miles'. What does that tell us about how each kind of tree moved?

tutor_only.confirm: Each kind of tree moved in its own clear way, so he could tell them apart from far off.
tutor_only.correct_reason: He says spruce, fir, pine and oak 'each had its own gesture', and that he could name a tree by that gesture at several miles.
tutor_only.tell: Every kind of tree had its own gesture, so he could name one from miles away.
help: The writer lists four kinds of tree as he says this.
Naming a tree from far off means its movement looked different from the others.
tutor_only.core_idea: Each kind of tree moved in its own clear way.
accept_ideas: each kind of tree moved in its own clear way
every species had a distinct gesture, so he could tell them apart
the trees did not all move the same way
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the trees all swayed together in the same way.
partial.ask: If every tree moved the same way, could he name one from miles off?

if_they_say.when: They say he knew the trees because he had studied them before.
if_they_say.ask: What in the moving forest let him name a tree from far away?

not_required: the names of the four trees
how long he stayed in the tree
tutor_only.full_idea: Each kind of tree moved in its own clear way, so the moving forest was not one blur.

items.prompt: From one leaf's click to trees miles away, what does that jump say about the wind?

tutor_only.confirm: It makes the wind one force across the whole range, not a gust in one tree.
tutor_only.correct_reason: He hears 'the small, hard click of one leaf against another,' then names trees 'at a distance of several miles,' so the same wind reaches from one leaf to the whole range.
tutor_only.tell: One leaf clicks, then miles of trees move, so one wind fills the range.
help: The click is one leaf. The later view is miles of trees.
Ask whether that is one wind or a gust in a single tree.
tutor_only.core_idea: The jump from one leaf to miles of trees makes the wind one force across the whole range, not a gust in one tree.
accept_ideas: one wind over miles of trees, not a gust in one leaf
the same wind fills the whole range
big enough to move every tree for miles
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the wind seems huge, loud, or like music, without saying it reaches from one leaf to miles of trees.
partial.ask: The click is one leaf. What is moving miles away?

partial.when: They say the wind was loud near him but quiet farther away.
partial.ask: Does the far view show the wind stopping, or reaching more trees?

if_they_say.when: They say the writer liked the sound of the leaves.
if_they_say.ask: What does the size of the change, from one leaf to miles, do to the wind?

items.prompt: By the end, what does the writer want the reader to feel about the storm?

tutor_only.confirm: That the storm is one huge force moving the whole range, and that it is worth staying out in.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The last part joins every separate sound into one and compares it to the sea, with every tree in the range answering the same wind.
tutor_only.tell: The single sounds join into one, and the forest answers the wind like a sea.
help: The writer stays in the tree for hours at the end.
He closes his eyes and says the sound is like the sea.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer wants the reader to feel the storm as one vast force that fills the whole range.
accept_ideas: the storm is one vast force filling the whole range
the storm is huge and wonderful, not only dangerous
the whole forest is moving as one thing
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the writer was frightened and wanted to climb down.
partial.ask: Does the writer leave the tree, or stay in it?

if_they_say.when: They say the storm was only a small wind in one valley.
if_they_say.ask: How much of the range is moving by the last part?
